title: Play
summary: Use play as relationship-building, reinforcement, confidence work, and impulse-control practice.

subcategories.title: Fetch Foundations — Bringing a Toy Back
subcategories.goal: Build a cooperative retrieve through small, rewarding steps.
subcategories.steps: Begin indoors with a toy your dog enjoys. Reward looking at, touching and picking up the toy, then gradually reward bringing it towards you. Start with the toy close by and add a short toss only once returning is enjoyable. Reward the return with food or another round of play.
subcategories.coachingNotes: Avoid chasing the dog or grabbing the toy from their mouth. Keep throws short on a non-slip surface and let the dog choose to participate. This is a game, so a formal retrieve is optional.

subcategories.title: Drop the Toy and Play Again
subcategories.goal: Teach a willing toy release that predicts another rewarding opportunity.
subcategories.steps: Practise with a low-excitement toy and tasty food. Say your chosen drop cue, offer a food reward and mark the release. Allow the dog to enjoy the toy again. Build a reliable response in easy sessions before asking for a release during more exciting play.
subcategories.coachingNotes: Do not prise open the mouth or pull the toy away. Return safe toys frequently so releasing does not always end the fun. If the dog freezes, guards or becomes worried, stop and ask your trainer for an individual plan.

subcategories.title: Cooperative Tug — Gentle Play and Pauses
subcategories.goal: Enjoy shared tug with comfortable movement and easy breaks.
subcategories.steps: Use a long, suitable tug toy and invite the dog to take the far end. Keep the game low to the ground with gentle movements. Practise short rounds, exchange the toy for food when a break is needed, and restart play as a reward for a comfortable release.
subcategories.coachingNotes: Keep all four paws on the ground and avoid lifting, jerking or twisting the dog. Let the dog win sometimes and invite them back. Reduce excitement if teeth approach hands or the dog has trouble taking a break.

subcategories.title: Take a Bow — A Playful Trick
subcategories.goal: Build a fun shared trick using gentle food guidance and rewards.
subcategories.steps: After the dog understands simple cues such as sit and down without visible food, begin from a comfortable stand. Use a treat near the nose to guide the head and chest gently down while the rear stays up. Reward small dips first, then gradually a deeper bow. Fade the food lure before adding a verbal cue.
subcategories.coachingNotes: Never push the body into position or hold the hips up. Use a non-slip surface and a comfortable range of movement. A trained bow is a trick and does not guarantee that the dog wants social play.

subcategories.title: Find It — Search for a Favourite Toy
subcategories.goal: Use a rewarding scent-search game for enjoyable mental activity.
subcategories.steps: Let the dog see you place a favourite toy in an easy spot nearby. Say Find it and allow them to explore. Celebrate finding it with a short game they enjoy. Gradually hide the toy partly out of sight, then increase the search area in small steps.
subcategories.coachingNotes: Use a helper if the dog has not learned to wait; avoid repeatedly testing a stay. Keep hiding places safe and accessible, help before frustration builds, and accept a slower pace. Sniffing should remain voluntary and enjoyable.
